newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean won ends down, sharp falls in afternoon.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean won ends down, sharp falls in afternoon.

text.p: The won closed lower versus the dollar on Wednesday with sharp falls spotted in late trading, traders said.
They said the won was now on a way down and expected further declines on Thursday. The won finished at 830.90 after opening at an intraday high of 827.00. It touched the low of 831.00.
U.S. President Bill Clinton's re-election didn't have much impact on the interbank market because it was widely expected.
Dealers said heavy dollar demand by an investment trust firm and speculative dollar buying pushed the local currency down.
A syndicate manager at Salomon Brothers in London said demand for the issue had mostly come from Japan and Asia.
"That's where most of the interest has been," he said, adding there had also been some demand from the Middle East and Europe and interest from U.S. investors as well.
He said Freddie Mac needed to launch callable structures to hedge their funding portfolios.
"There's an ongoging need for Freddie Mac and we've been able to respond because we've identified Asian demand," he said.
In the sterling sector, Anglian Water set a 150 million stg 10-year bond via joint lead managers BZW and J.P. Morgan Securities which was later priced to yield 52 b.p. over gilts.
Anglian finance director Chris Mellor was reported to say uncertainty over short-term interest rates made a bond issue attractive. The utility last issued bonds in 1990.

Later, Standard & Poor's Corp assigned the issue an AA minus senior unsecured rating. "Anglian's robust financial profile and stable operating environment should provide the company with a fair degree of insulation from the impact of key regulatory and political event risks going forward," the agency said.
"Nonetheless, the potential for a sudden decline in credit quality still exists should a takeover of aggressive windfall tax on utilities materialise in the future," S&P said.
A syndicate manager at J.P. Morgan said they had been over-subscribed for the issue. "It has gone very well," he said.
"Water paper is popular, there is not a lot of it, it is viewed as less risky than electricity paper and there has been strong UK buying," he said.
"There has also been demand out of Japan and Asia, France, Germany, Switzerland, Benelux and Scandanavia as well as interest from the Middle East."
Following Walt Disney's first foray into the New Zealand dollar sector on Tuesday, the World Bank set a NZ$100 million one-year bond which pays a 7.25 percent coupon.
While Commerzbank launched a NZ$100 million three-year bond which paid a 7.25 percent coupon.
